sports.title: Clock operator robbed Bengals of one final play
sports.summary: The Bengals-Commanders game carries a small but not insignificant asterisk.
sports.body:
As ESPN rules analyst Russell Yurk explained in the postgame show, the clock operator incorrectly ran the remaining four seconds off the clock during the game-winning field goal from Washington.

Yurk said two seconds remained when the ball hit the net. It looks more like it should have been one second.

Regardless, Yurk said the replay process can’t restore time when the next play isn’t a scrimmage play. (There’s also a rule regarding restoring time when there are fewer than two seconds left, and — with all due respect to Yurk — it appears that there was only one second when the ball hit the net.)

The bottom line is that the clock operator was slow to get to the button, and there wasn’t anything that could be done about it.

What would have happened if the Bengals had gotten one last chance? We’ll never know, because the person hired to keep track of the time handled it incorrectly.

Or, depending on that person’s rooting interests, he handled it perfectly.

sports.title: Monday Night Football: Commanders rally for 22-20 win over Bengals
sports.summary: There were no late mistakes for the Commanders this time.
sports.body:
After a 56-yard field goal by Evan McPherson put the Bengals up 20-19, the Commanders took possession on their own 28-yard line with 46 seconds left to play. Jayden Daniels hit rookie wideout Antonio Williams with a pair of passes that covered 64 yards and exorcised the demons from their tie with the Giants by spiking the ball with time left for Drew Stevens to try a 26-yard field goal.

Stevens knocked it through the uprights and the Commanders were 22-20 winners on their home field. It’s the second straight win for the Commanders and the end of a five-game winning streak for the Bengals.

Daniels was 23-of-35 for 289 yards and the Commanders scored on six straight drives after opening the game with four punts on four possessions. The final five of those drives ended with Stevens field goals, but the Commanders dominated time of possession in the final 30 minutes.

Their run game had a big hand in that. Jacory Croskey-Merritt had 13 carries for 54 yards and a touchdown and Daniels had a 47-yard run to set up one of Stevens’s kicks. Williams led all receivers with nine catches for 122 yards, but the Commanders remained in position to pull out the win thanks to their defense.

The Bengals were limited to 124 yards in the second half and they punted twice after taking a 17-10 lead in the third quarter. Joe Burrow finished with 300 passing yards, but the big plays that were the hallmark of their winning streak didn’t develop against a Commanders defense that limited Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins to seven catches for 74 yards.

Washington improved to 4-5-1 with the win and they have to feel good about their chances of sticking around the NFC East race with games against the Cardinals and Titans on tap in the next two weeks. The Giants finished Week 11 at 6-3-1 and the Cowboys are 5-6.

The Bengals are now 7-3, which leaves them a game clear of both the Browns and Steelers in the AFC North. They split their season series with the Steelers and still have both games against the Browns on their upcoming schedule, but their immediate focus will be on next Sunday’s game against the Saints.

sports.title: SEC plans to consider ejecting LSU on December 3
sports.summary: The supposed "chaos" in college sports could still result in the SEC kicking LSU out of the conference.
sports.body:
Via Mark Schlabach of ESPN, the conference plans to consider giving LSU the boot at a meeting on December 3.

The disclosure came in court papers filed Monday in connection with a legal battle arising from LSU’s placement of guard RJ Luis Jr. on the roster, after he played in preseason games for the Boston Celtics.

“The lawsuit seeks to protect the Conference’s ability to govern itself and to enforce the rules and policies its member universities have voluntarily adopted,” the SEC said in a statement. “The Conference maintains its right to associate only with institutions that meet its established standards and expectations of membership and that demonstrate appropriate institutional control of their athletics programs.”

The fight first emerged when the LSU football team considered adding to the roster players who had spots on 90-man NFL rosters in the offseason, training camp, and preseason. LSU eventually backed down.

The overriding question is whether players who have signed what are essentially tryout contract are “professional” players. And whether college athletes who are now being paid are not “professional.”

The entire dynamic arises from players making the strategic decision to pursue opportunities deemed to be more lucrative. College athletes in the high-revenue sports are essentially pro players. The fact that a small handful of players who have attempted to become pro players have chosen to return to college for business reasons creates a convenient — but disingenuous — talking point.

It’s easy, and phony, to frame it as “pro players” returning to college. They’re ALL pro players at this point, even if the NCAA and its members continue to covet an antitrust exemption that will allow them to restrict the amount of money the players can make, thereby diverting the finite booster funds toward the program, and the coaches.

It’s really that simple. The powers-that-be want to reduce the revenue stream for player, because that money can otherwise be funneled to the schools. But they won’t admit that, because that makes it harder to get public (and in turn political) support. It’s easier to frame it as “pro players playing in college sports.”

ESPN cameras caught Diggs on the sideline, angrily telling someone, “ Throw the fucking ball !”

Presumably, Diggs’s frustrations were targeted at the player who is responsible for throwing the ball — quarterback Jayden Daniels.

The display from Diggs is part of the price of having him on the team. Whether it’s passion to win or selfishness or something in between, he’s fiery. He’s feisty. And it’s part of the price of having him on the team.

The good news is that, the first time the Commanders got the ball after Diggs had his sideline outburst, Daniels engineered a touchdown drive that narrowed the deficit to 10-7.

Still, it makes plenty of sense in the second half to pay attention to Diggs. It’s not the first time he has flashed in-game frustration, and it’s surely not the last.

sports.title: Tee Higgins touchdown highlights inconsistency of replay review
sports.summary: Just when we thought we were out when it comes to not knowing what a catch is, they pull us back in.
sports.body:
The past two days have included three examples of plays that make more confusing the question of whether a player has completed the act of catching the ball — and whether replay review was properly used to correct rulings made on the field.

It started on Sunday afternoon, when an apparent touchdown catch by Jaguars receiver Parker Washington was ruled not a catch on the field, with replay review not overturning the ruling. Even though the visual evidence seemed to provide clear and obvious proof that the ball was caught.

On Sunday night, 49ers receiver Mike Evans bobbled his way to a touchdown catch . He quite possibly didn’t get two feet in bounds after finally securing control of the ball. The play wasn’t even reviewed.

On Monday night, Bengals receiver Tee Higgins made a touchdown catch even though the ball was moving as he landed on the ground and out of bounds. There was no replay review.

The common denominator in these plays (beyond the fact that they involved potential touchdown catches) is the shadowy, uncertain replay process. As one head coach explained it to PFT on Monday (before the Bengals-Commanders game), it’s still not known who is making the decisions in New York as to what will be reviewed and what the outcome of the review will be.

It’s another reason for the NFL to embrace full transparency when it comes to replay review. We need to know who is making the decisions. We need to know their names. We need to hear their voices.

And we also need to know why — as happened in the case of the Evans and Higgins touchdowns — there was no full-blown review.

sports.title: Monday Night Football: Bengals lead 10-7 at halftime
sports.summary: Both offenses took some time to get going on a rainy night in Washington.
sports.body:
After a 15-play drive resulted in a field goal midway through the second quarter, the Bengals found more explosive plays on their next possession. Running back Samaje Perine broke free on a short pass for a 44-yard gain and Joe Burrow then went deep to wide receiver Tee Higgins for a 31-yard touchdown on the first play after the two-minute warning. The catch bore some resemblance to the one by Jaguars wideout Parker Washington that was ruled incomplete on Sunday, but there was no review.

That score put the Bengals up 10-0 and left the Commanders with a last chance to find their first points of the evening.

Jayden Daniels ran for one first down and threw for two more before hooking up with tight end Chig Okonkwo for a 32-yard gain that moved the Commanders to Cincinnati’s 6-yard-line. A pass to wide receiver Treylon Burks in the end zone drew a pass interference flag on cornerback Dax Hill and running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt punched the ball in on the next play to make it 10-7 going into the break.

Daniels is 8-of-11 for 85 yards, but has been sacked three times by Boye Mafe. The last of those came on a third down and led to an animated Stefon Diggs appearing to yell about throwing the ball on the sideline while the Bengals had possession. Diggs’s only catch of the half came on the late touchdown drive.

Burrow is 16-of-23 for 179 yards and has been sacked a couple of times. The Bengals also saw safety Bryan Cook leave just before halftime with an ankle injury and he’s called questionable to be back on the field when the Commanders get the ball to start the second half.

sports.title: Bengals get on the board in second quarter, lead 3-0

sports.body:

It was a 15-play drive covering 71 yards for Cincinnati and the workmanlike grind illustrates the lack of explosive plays for one of the league’s top offenses.

The Bengals punted the first two times they had the ball and their third drive ended after Samaje Perine and Joe Burrow were both stuffed for no gain on third and fourth down. The Commanders took over in Bengals territory, but Boye Mafe’s second sack of the first half led to their third punt of the night.

sports.title: Making sense of Liam Coen's nonsensical decision to kick a late field goal
sports.summary: Jacksonville's loss to the Giants on Sunday included a nonsensical decision with 3:43 to play.
sports.body:
After the game, Jaguars coach Liam Coen justified the decision to take the three points by calling an effort to score a touchdown a “ hope play .”

We hope he’s not serious. It was eight yards, not 80. Regardless of what the analytics said, it was time to go for the touchdown, which with a successful two-point conversion would have tied the game.

As explained on Monday’s PFT Live , I think the two-point conversion was the deciding factor for Coen. When the score was 23-9, the Jaguars scored a touchdown that cut the margin to eight. After the touchdown, Coen played the all-too-common analytics game, opting to go for two in the hopes of cutting the margin to six and ideally avoiding overtime if they had scored again.

When it was time to go for two, Coen utilized his best two-point play based on the specific matchup of the Jacksonville offense against the New York defense. It failed. Which meant that, if/when the Jaguars scored another touchdown, they would need to rely on Coen’s second-best two-point play.

After Plan A failed, why would Coen believe Plan B would succeed?

And so instead of going for a touchdown which may or may not have been capped by a successful two-point try, Coen opted to take the three and kick off. Which pissed off the New York offense , and which helped set the stage for the Jaguars never getting the ball again.

If the Jaguars had gone for the score, the Giants would have gotten the ball deep in their own end. The Jaguars would have been likely to get another shot at a touchdown and a two-point conversion.

Still, the Jaguars would have had to convert a two-point play after their best option at going for two had failed. In the moment, that reality may have been the difference for Coen.

sports.title: Mike McCarthy: Aaron Rodgers is our quarterback
sports.summary: Before an NFL team benches its starting quarterback, someone asks the coach whether the quarterback could be benched.
sports.body:
That happened for the first time during Aaron Rodgers’s two-year tenure with the team on Monday, during a press conference with coach Mike McCarthy, one day after the team’s latest loss, to the Eagles.

It came up as innocuously as possible. McCarthy wasn’t asked whether Rodgers could get the hook; McCarthy was asked whether he’s considering using one of the other three quarterbacks on the roster in an effort to mix things up when the offense is struggling.

Of course he is. Even if Rodgers’s play merits benching, Aaron Rodgers isn’t getting benched. It’s implicit in the arrangement.

Still, Aaron Rodgers is a far cry from what he once was. In 10 games this season, Rodgers has completed 220 of 361 passes for 2,241 yards, with 16 touchdown passes and six interceptions. His passer rating of 86.6 is the lowest of his career since becoming Green Bay’s starter in 2008, with the exception of a four-snap performance in 2023 with the Jets (39.6, based on one incomplete pass thrown).

At 6-4, the Steelers remain in contention for another one-and-out playoff appearance. That makes it easier to justify staying the course. With upcoming games against the Broncos, Texans, and Jaguars, that could change.

Even then, Rodgers would never be benched. He’d be “injured.” And his career would end not with a bang but with a whimper.

sports.title: Report: NFL Primetime documentary is in the works
sports.summary: The recent passing of Tom Jackson has sparked much discussion about ESPN's NFL Primetime, which was for years a mandatory Sunday evening destination for football fans everywhere.
sports.body:
As it turns out, a documentary is coming regarding the show.

Via Sam Neumann of Awful Announcing , the final product is believed to be on track for a release in connection with the Super Bowl, which is being televised by ESPN and ABC.

It could be part of the game-day programming. Three years ago, CBS debuted You Are Looking Live! — a documentary about The NFL Today — before the launch of the official pregame show in advance of Super Bowl LVIII.

For those who were actively following the NFL in the late ‘80s, NFL Primetime provided the first opportunity to see extended highlights of NFL games on the day they were played. Years before the Internet, social media, Sunday Ticket, and RedZone, Primetime became appointment viewing for fans who wanted to see more about what was happening beyond the two or three games available in their local markets on Sunday afternoon.

And the team of Chris Berman and Tom Jackson became the tour guides for the opportunity to essentially watch all of the important plays from every game in a compressed but meaningful package, with Berman’s cadence and the music accompanying the words creating the loose impression that it was all happening live. Even though everyone knew it wasn’t.

It became a unique moment in time, which at the time didn’t seem to have a shelf life. It’s just the way things were, with fans having no concept that there would ever be a way to watch all of the games live or to see any and all relevant plays long before 7:00 p.m. ET. It was a new frontier that no one had reason to believe would not remain a permanent fixture of each and every NFL Sunday.

As Neumann explains it, Jackson recently made a surprise return to ESPN as part of the filming of the documentary. ESPN shared footage of the reunion on Sunday.

It’s worth your time to watch it, if you were one of the millions who climbed aboard the Primetime Express every Sunday night of football season for something much more meaningful than a glimpse of the entire day of NFL action. And the documentary will undoubtedly bring back fond memories of the final years before advances in technology caused a narrow range of football options to explode into today’s endless menu of choices.

sports.title: Bears have gone five straight games without ever trailing for first time since 1985
sports.summary: The Bears' win over the Saints on Sunday was their fifth consecutive game taking a first-quarter lead and winning without ever trailing.
sports.body:
The last Bears team to win five straight games without ever trailing was the 1985 Bears, one of the most dominant teams in NFL history.

That 1985 Bears team lost just one game, a Monday night classic against the Dolphins in the 13th game of the season, and after that loss to the Dolphins they never trailed in the final three games of the regular season, or in the two playoff games they won to earn a trip to Super Bowl XX. In the Super Bowl, the Bears fell behind 3-0 in the first quarter before winning 46-10, snapping their streak of five straight games without trailing.

This Bears team isn’t dominating quite like that 1985 team, but the Bears are currently on a very impressive run: They haven’t just won five games in a row, but they’ve scored in every quarter of all five games, the franchise’s first streak of 20 consecutive quarters scoring since the 1941 Bears. That team, like the 1985 team, won the NFL championship.

The 2026 Bears are playing like some of the best teams in franchise history. They’re jumping out to early leads and never looking back.

sports.title: Colts-Texans draws tepid 12.23 million on Thursday night
sports.summary: No, they can't all be winners.
sports.body:
NFL viewership is driven largely by quality of matchup. The Thursday night matchup that launched Week 11 may have driven some viewers to examine their life choices.

Still, 12.23 million watched the game between the Colts and Texans, on average. It was the smallest Thursday night audience of the season, and it represented a nine-percent drop from last year’s Week 11 Thursday night game between the Jets and Patriots.

The game also faced competition from the release of the new Grand Theft Auto video game.

The latest game dragged the full-season average under 17 million for the first time this year. It now stands at 16.62 million per game.

The Prime Video schedule concludes with Broncos at Steelers on Black Friday, Chiefs at Rams on December 3, Vikings at Patriots on December 10, 49ers at Chargers on December 17, Texans at Eagles on December 24, and Ravens at Bengals on December 31.

Flexing is an option for some of those contests. The window opens in Week 13, with the move “generally” coming no later than 21 days before the date of the game.

At this point, Vikings-Patriots is only 17 days away. Flexing remains possible for the final three games — with 49ers-Chargers possibly on the brink of being moved. The Week 15 Sunday schedule otherwise includes Bengals-Panthers, Browns-Giants, and Cowboys-Rams.

sports.title: Terrion Arnold's lawyer seeks sanctions for discovery violation
sports.summary: Seahawks cornerback Terrion Arnold remains on paid leave with eight felony charges pending in Florida.
sports.body:
On Monday, attorney Harvey Steinberg filed a motion for sanctions, arising from the alleged failure of the prosecution to timely disclose as discovery material.

The gist of the 13-page filing is that the prosecution withheld a statement from defendant Boakai Hilton until after another defendant, Arianna Del Valle, sat for a sworn, pre-trial deposition.

Hilton’s statement, per the filing, conflicts with statements made by Del Valle. By not having the Hilton statement, Steinberg was unable to properly question Del Valle about the discrepancies.

On the surface, it’s an easy fix. Steinberg should get another chance to question Del Valle under oath. At a deeper level, the situation (if it unfolded the way Steinberg alleges) speaks to the integrity of the process.

Prosecutors have immense power and discretion, which should be exercised at all times with the goal of doing justice. Sometimes, a blind desire to “win” can overcome the mandate to do justice, thereby corrupting the system.

The Hillsborough County prosecutor’s office is already dealing with an unrelated case in which “winning” may have trumped justice. A prosecutor recently resigned for failing to disclose during jury selection that the sister of a fellow prosecutor was in the jury pool for a rape trial. The woman ultimately served as the foreperson of the jury, which returned a conviction.

A new trial has been ordered, and the prosecutor who failed to disclose the relationship has resigned.

It all comes back to integrity. Are the prosecutors playing games in order get a conviction or a favorable plea deal, or are the prosecutors committed to justice in whatever form it may take?

sports.body: I think part of being a diehard NFL fan is trying to derive meaning out of everything that happens to a team, no matter how small. Think about the offseason program. How often do we have reports on which players are up and which players are down? These continue into training camp. Then the second half of preseason games produce deep dive analysis of which players are potentially hidden gems or important depth pieces. Every now and then an OTA, training camp, or preseason, breakout turns out to be a preview of a genuine step forward by a developing player. Far more often the players and the hype are forgotten. It also goes this way in late season games when a team has fallen out of the Playoff race. Can a loss help a team secure a high Draft pick to land a franchise changing player? Can a late season surge lead to momentum carrying into a future season and be the first step in instilling a new culture? In both cases the answer is yes. Far more often, however, these games don’t have a ton of meaning either way in the long run. They amount to a bad team playing out the string. The Jets’ Week 11 victory over the Chargers has evoked passions across the fanbase. Some fans are furious about the team hurting its NFL Draft positioning. Others are happy to get the win. I don’t think there’s a “right” or a “wrong” way to be a fan. Everybody wants the same thing in the end, for the Jets to have success. Opinions simply vary on the best way to get there. I can understand fans who are hoping for as high of a pick as possible. Of course, we have seen over and over that the quality of the coaching staff and front office making the pick are generally far more important than where the pick is made. Patrick Mahomes, Josh Allen, and Lamar Jackson were not the first quarterbacks selected in their respective Draft years. Taking it deeper, one study suggests the odds of the top player drafted at his position having a better career than the third player picked at the same position is only slightly better than a coin toss. Yes, there is the occasional case where losing helps a team land a player who legitimately changes everything, and there are cases where a meaningless late season win causes a team to miss out on that player. sports.body: The Buffalo Bills beat the Dolphinss 26-9 in Week 11 at Highmark Stadium, in a game that was far from perfection from Joe Brady’s but felt more impressive than last week’s win over the Jets. The Bills are now 9-1. These are my takeaways from Buffalo’s victory. Josh Allen came out ready to let it rip And I loved it. Not necessarily because Allen always made the “right” decision determining at which level to throw the football. I want defenses to be forced to think about all possible variations of Buffalo’s offense. And Allen is the best player in football. The Bills slammed their foot on the gas pedal to begin this game, and while it didn’t amount to something like three-consecutive touchdown drives — which we’ve certainly witnessed during the Allen era — it led to three pass plays of 20-plus yards and two touchdowns in the first half as Buffalo built its lead. Allen seemed adamant about dicing the Dolphins secondary through the air, and not underneath. That is Allen being Allen. Allen didn’t have a carry against the Dolphins, which now amounts to, ironically, a similar place to where we were after the Patriots loss, when the Allen criticism centered around him throwing it downfield too frequently and not running nearly enough. And what happened after that? Allen averaged 11.1 yards per attempt and ran for 121 yards on 10 carries in a 37-34 win on the road against the Rams. The safety group has become a strength Amazing, right? Even if you don’t fully agree with me, it’s impossible it ignore the difference in the play of this group recently compared to the first month or so of the season. Cole Bishop is so perfectly positioned in his box/blitz role that asks him to cover the slot underneath. He’s become a weapon as an addition to the pass rush, and his size plus explosiveness and strength allow the Bills to defend the run respectably in dime, if needed. Good early returns on Amani Hooker, as he’s allowed four catches for 47 yards with two pass breakups, nine total tackles, and a quarterback hit on three pass-rush snaps in his two contests with the Bills. And, heck, new safety No. 3, Damar Hamlin, had the biggest splash play of the group against Miami, an impressive interception at the intermediate level. Jordan Hancock played outstandingly in the safety/slot hybrid role, and the Bills even got Jalon Kilgore and Sam Franklin Jr. onto the field in this contest.

sports.summary: Buffalo Bills running back James Cook III has spent much of the 2026 season putting together one of the most consistent stretches of rushing production in NFL history. sports.body: Buffalo Bills running back James Cook III has spent much of the 2026 season putting together one of the most consistent stretches of rushing production in NFL history. With another strong performance against the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, Cook now has a place on the all-time leaderboard all to himself. With Sunday’s performance, which included 89 rushing yards and a touchdown, Cook became just the second player in NFL history to rush for at least 75 yards and score a rushing touchdown in nine consecutive games, moving past three former NFL running backs who had each reached eight straight. Notably, he’s the only player in league history to put up those numbers in one season. [Media: https://twitter.com/BuffaloBillsPR/status/2124605029529403539?a=SI4XCAzJ3357jRKxHXM&s=20] Cook entered the game tied with Pro Football Hall of Famers John Riggins and LaDainian Tomlinson, along with George Rogers, for the second-longest streak in NFL history. Riggins accomplished the feat in 1983, Rogers did it across the 1985 and 1986 seasons, and Tomlinson matched them in 2006. The 27-year-old Cook joined that group during Buffalo’s Week 10 victory over the New York Jets. He rushed for 157 yards on 18 carries, including a career-long 74-yard touchdown run in the second half of the Bills’ 31-12 win. Now, only Terry Allen stands ahead of Cook. Allen reached 10 consecutive games with at least 75 rushing yards and a touchdown while playing for Washington across the 1995 and 1996 seasons. With nine straight games behind him, Cook is now within striking distance of a record that’s stood for 30 years, but the road won’t get any easier. Kansas City and New England are next on Buffalo’s schedule, and the dates next to those names are just as challenging as the opponents. The Bills have just three days to rest, recover, and prepare to host the Chiefs on Thanksgiving night. If Cook is going to catch Terry Allen, he’ll have to keep his streak alive through one of the toughest stretches of Buffalo’s season.

Is it too early to start throwing around the word legendary? Maybe, but Rousseau is certainly making a case for it. With two sacks against the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, Rousseau has officially entered uncharted territory in his NFL career. His 10 sacks this season are a new personal best. [Media: https://twitter.com/BuffaloBillsPR/status/2124568810426356152?a=PKP5mAXAD9DcankXAG0&s=20] Rousseau sacked Miami quarterback Kyle McCord for an eight-yard loss that forced the Dolphins to punt after a five-play first drive. [Media: https://twitter.com/BuffaloBillsPR/status/2124585141821452485?a=LnRiXda6MHK5TN5rwfs&s=20] Rousseau entered the NFL in 2021 as a defensive end, spending his first five seasons in Sean McDermott’s defensive system. Along the way, he worked under Leslie Frazier, McDermott himself, and Bobby Babich as defensive leaders, while learning from defensive line coaches Eric Washington and Marcus West. Then came 2026, and just about everything changed. Jim Leonhard took over as defensive coordinator, bringing a new scheme that moved Rousseau from defensive end to outside linebacker. Bobby April III became his new position coach, giving Rousseau his third position coach and fourth defensive leader in six NFL seasons. Somehow, through all that change, Rousseau is putting together the most productive season of his career. sports.body: In the New York Jets’ 11th game of the 2026 season, in Los Angeles, California, the Jets beat the Los Angeles Chargers, 27 - 24. The game opened with the Jets on offense. They moved down the field with their running game and a completion to Adonai Mitchell before the drive bogged down. The Jets settled for a doinked 50 yard field goal that sneaked through the uprights for an early 3 - 0 Jets lead. The pattern of settling for field goals that persisted the last couple of weeks continued on the first drive of the game. The Chargers answered with a field goal drive of their own and the game was tied at 3 - 3 late in the first quarter. The Jets answered with a long drive featuring the running game. As the first quarter ended the Jets had a third and three at the Chargers 12 yard line. Three plays later the Jets were in the end zone as Geno Smith hit Breece Hall for the Jets’ first touchdown in 10 quarters. The Jets had a 10 - 3 lead early in the second quarter. After the Jets stopped the Chargers when David Bailey shut down the drive with a strip sack, the Jets offense took over. They quickly drove down the field with a nice mix of runs and passes. The drive ended when Geno Smith found Sterling Shepard, fresh off the practice squad, for a touchdown and a 17 - 3 Jets lead late in the second quarter. The Chargers closed out the second quarter with a drive ending in a Justin Herbert touchdown run as time expired in the first half. The drive was aided at the end by a bogus roughing the passer call on David Bailey. The Jets went into the locker room leading the Chargers 17 - 10. The Jets opened the third quarter on defense. After the Jets shut down the Chargers with the help of another David Bailey sack, the Jets offense took over.
